speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the speech from the throne and the addresses made by the leaders of this house upon that subject are so comprehensive in character and so all-embracing in the number and importance of the matters discussed that it is impossible for any man in the space of forty minutes to deal with them as a whole. Therefore I make no apology for confining myself at this time to one phase of the situation as we find it in this country, and to one reference in the speech itself. I refer to the Natural Products Marketing Act, to the attitude of the producers towards that act as far as I have been able to ascertain that attitude, and to the plans which thus far have been brought forward and presented by the producers under its provisions.
Lest I should be challenged as to my familiarity with that subject may I make this brief statement; upon my return home after prorogation, I found interest among the producers so intense that in view of some familiarity on my part with the bill itself I was in receipt of numerous invitations to speak on the subject throughout the west, particularly in Alberta, and I availed myself of as many of those invitations as was possible. In addition I have had the pleasure of being associated with various committees and boards which the producers themselves set up in Alberta and throughout the west for the preparation and presentation of their plans, and I have taken part in their discussion and consideration. At the request of the poultry producers of the three prairie provinces and of the live stock producers of Alberta I have assisted in presenting those plans before the federal board in Ottawa. I make this statement for one purpose and one only, which is to indicate that I have had some opportunity of acquainting myself with the general reaction amongst the producers in respect to this act, and with the work done and the plans in process and in contemplation by the producers under the provisions of the legislation.

Wherever you go throughout Canada to-day among the farming population, and certainly in the province of Alberta and throughout the west generally, you find this question being, asked, and asked with increasing interest and increasing vehemence:	Why it is that during,
this and all depressions, when general business-is curtailed and meets difficulties through restriction of sales and through falling prices, the agricultural industry and agricultural products have been the greatest sufferers? This question does not embody an argument; it embodies a statement of fact. It is generally recognized that the farming population has suffered more than others not only in the falling of prices but in something which is more important, namely the relative exchange value of their products when translated into terms of those goods and services which they must purchase. It makes comparatively little difference, apart from the payment of debt and interest, whether wheat, for instance is fifty cents a bushel or two dollars; what counts is how many bushels of wheat it takes to purchase a given quantity of machinery, of household effects, of personal necessities. That is the question that is asked. It was in seeking an answer to that question that I believe this act v'as introduced, and it was because of that question that this intense interest has been aroused amongst the producers themselves. In the opinion of most of those definitely and directly affected, the chief factor which has brought about that differentiation and that lack of parity in exchange value is that during modern times there has been a disposition on the part of most productive enterprises gradually to centralize the control of their operations. The merging of small factories into larger, the centralization of production and control has proceeded. With this I am not quarel-ling; it may be sound; it may be in the interest of efficiency; at any rate it certainly is the tendency at the present time. But you find this also, that as business becomes centralized, and as the controlling executives of the various industries become fewer and fewer, it becomes more and more simple for them to control by agreement both the production and the merchandising policies of their industries. And because of that they have been able to withstand, in some degree at least, the shock of the depression in relation to their price levels.
Now we turn to agriculture. Whatever the future may bring-and I am no prophet-up to the present time as far as we can ascertain the individually owned and operated farm has been the most efficient form of agriculture; it certainly is the one most in vogue in this

The Address-Mr. Speakman
country and on the North American continent. With that also I have no quarrel, but based on that fact we find this, that throughout the prairie provinces alone there are scores of thousands of individuals who themselves control not only their production policy but their merchandising policy also. You find also- and again this is not stated as argument but admitted and acknowledged as fact-that when this is the position the basic price of the commodity produced is set not by the strongest man, the man most competent in merchandising, the man who financially is best able to choose the time and manner of his sales, but by the weakest man, the man who is forced to sell and who may be driven to the lowest possible price. The price he will accept controls the basic price of the entire production. Upon the recognition of this fact was based the response of western Canada at least, and the producers of western Canada, to this act. They saw in it a possibility of removing that disability by their own effort and of placing themselves on a parity as far as sales management is concerned with those industries with which they must do business.
The act itself I shall not discuss, for every member of this house is familiar with its terms and provisions. The charge has been made that it is complex, that it is drastic, and that it is an interference by the state with the personal rights and personal business of individuals. Yet if properly understood the principles of this act and of all the plans formulated and brought forward under it are neither complex nor difficult. They embrace one principle, which is this-I will put it in the form of a question: Is there any productive industry in Canada outside of agriculture which is without a sales department as a part of that industry, functioning in the interest of that industry, and disposing of the product of that industry to the distributing trade? I think the answer will be that there is none. Indeed, I think it will be admitted by those engaged in other industries that they could not possibly function without such a sales department. Imagine for a moment every manager of every branch factory of some great manufacturing industry making sales to the trade on his own initiative, without coordination, without executive control, each manager of each unit and branch competing with the other units and managers in the same industry for the sales to be made. The answer would be that such a situation would bring about bankruptcy. Then, when we turn to agriculture we find that there are not a few unit branches, not a few independent managers, but scores of thousands of independent managers each making his own independent sales with
results such as I have indicated. That is the principle of the act, and the principle of every plan so far formulated under the act, namely to create for the agricultural industry sales departments which will place that industry upon a parity with others with which it must do business. At the present time I am referring only to agriculture, but I have in mind the fact that the act is possible of broader implications.
Of the plans thus far brought forward I think that the two presented from western Canada-and I say western Canada advisedly because the three prairie provinces are embraced-are perhaps by far the most important, the most comprehensive and most allembracing. As a matter of fact it is not too much to say that the poultry plan which was the first to be presented on the part of all three prairie provinces was the first plan brought forward under the act taking advantage of all its provisions. I believe when the plan is outlined it will commend itself to the sympathetic understanding of every hon. member. The producers found many difficulties: they were largely unorganized: they were without full knowledge of what the act implied and in many cases they had no basis upon which to commence their operations. In each of those provinces what were known as provisional boards or committees were set up. In some instances the movement was inaugurated by the pools then in existence. In other instances, as happened in Alberta, the Minister of Agriculture in that province was asked after discussion with and in cooperation with the various organizations in the poultry industry to appoint a board which would be representative of the industry as a whole. To this board certain limited functions were allocated, namely to prepare a plan, to organize at least in some degree, to call a meeting of the producers themselves and to lay before that body either for endorsation or rejection the plan they had formulated. This took place and in each case-and I say "in each case" advisedly-the plans were identical in form, because each of the three prairie provinces recognize the fact that their problems are the same and that their organizations must extend beyond the bounds of their own territory. Those plans were presented to the bodies of poultry men, the men and women engaged in the poultry business, and in each case received the almost unanimous endorsation of the assemblies.
Then another step could be taken. Those gatherings authorized the temporary or provisional boards to make the initial presentation of their plans to the federal board in
The Address-Mr. Speakman

Ottawa, and eventually the plans were presented. They were scanned and examined; they were submitted to the law officers of the crown; they were approved as being sound and practical; they were approved as being within the provisions of the act and therefore legal. Then, referring to the poultry plan, in order that absolute fairness might be observed, a period was set aside for public advertisement during which time anyone in opposition to the plan or anyone who might have an amendment to suggest was invited to present his opposition or amendment before the federal board. At the conclusion of that period another hearing was held at which those opposed were invited to be present and indeed were present. The plans were again discussed in the light of representations made, and after some changes in wording and some slight amendments, were given final approval by the board.
I think hon. members will agree with me that up to that point the utmost fairness and the soundest business practice was followed. Then the question arose as to whether or not those plans did or did not have the real approval of the producers themselves. It followed that the local boards, the bodies responsible for the introduction and presentation of the plans, asked that an opportunity to cast a vote should be given to every producer whose product had come under the operation of the plan. In this arrangement the minister concurred. An order in council was to be passed which would create under the terms of the act what would be known as a registered producer. In the case of the poultry producers every poultryman in the three prairie provinces having a flock of twenty-five birds or more would be included; in other words every producer whose product might be subject to the plan would be affected. The list having been prepared a proclamation would be issued. Every producer within the provinces whose product would be affected would be given ample opportunity to register, thus attaining a threefold objective: first, to designate those whose products would be handled by the boards; second, to provide on the same basis a list of those ivho would be entitled to vote, and third, in the event of a plan coming into operation, to provide a definite summary or definite detailed statement of the amount of poultry products which might be raised or sold from every farm in western Canada. As I understand it arrangements have now been made under which the producers will be entitled to vote by ballot under the jurisdiction not of an interested party, not of those i Mr. Speakman. 1
who have organized the plans, but of a tribunal set up and created by the government, as in every other election or provision which is made for voting. I believe no one may cavil at the fairness of the proposal. Now the promoters themselves have asked that only after a substantial majority of the producers pronounce themselves in favour of the plan shall such plan come into effect.
The live stock men followed a somewhat similar procedure. I might add, however, that in these plans each province will have a local board to be elected and reelected by the producers. The three provinces will then combine to create a sales agency which they shall control, and which shall designate and carry into effect the various sales policies of the producers. As to live stock a similar plan was followed, the minister was asked again to appoint a board of fifteen or seventeen men representative of every phase of the live stock industry. In that connection something happened which might almost be called a minor miracle-of course I am speaking more particularly of Alberta although the plans in Saskatchewan are on identically the same terms. Hon. members who are familiar with the history of the live stock industry know that there has always been a complete lack of understanding between the individual producers, the large ranchers and the small cooperatively organized farmers. I was delighted to see this board, composed of representatives of the largest live stock producers in Alberta or in Canada, representatives of the cooperatives, of the breeders' and feeders' associations, agree unanimously as to the objectives to be achieved and the plans to be effected. This committee devised a plan under which they hope their business may be operated. When that had been done a public meeting was called in the city of Calgary to which something like 160 live stock associations in that province were invited to send delegates. There were present some two hundred delegates representing about 140 organizations and about thirty or forty of the largest individual ranchers, and by a vote of 195 to 5 they approved of the plan and empowered the provisional committee to present that plan before the federal board That will indicate, Mr. Speaker, the steps which have been taken and the unanimity which has prevailed throughout those industries in respect of this undertaking.
These producers have in mind certain objectives, which are very clearly defined. They may be stated in a sentence: to create in that department of the industry a sales department which for the first time will

The Address-Mr. Speakman
function in the interests of the industry, and give the producers an effective voice in the sale and in the manner of the sale of their products.
It has been suggested that this is wholly unnecessary, that the present system, with a little control, a little checking, a little renovating, will amply serve its purpose. May I place before the house one illustration of the situation as it exists?-for I shall not labour the point. It is an illustration that is familiar to every member of this house and to every producer in Canada. Thirty-five years ago as a young man I was in the business of raising cattle and I sold my cattle, as everyone did in those days, on the one basis of $30 a head for three-3-ear old steers on the hoof, and we sold them by the bunch. That was the basic price which was graded down for females and small stuff. A short time ago one of my neighbours who has been raising that class of beef cattle for forty-five years made a sale, and he netted $15 for three-year old steers of the same class and quality that thirty-five years ago brought $30. So in thirty-five years the price of that product has fallen by one-half, while in the same time the cost of producing these animals has doubled. Thirty-five years ago we raised our stock on the open range and to-day they are raised upon privately owned and municipally taxed land, and. as well, the price of many of the things that we must purchase from our proceeds has greatly risen.
I think the house and the country will perceive at once that no industry cau carry on under those conditions, and that for us to remain in our present position is intolerable and impossible. The conditions in part, of course, are beyond our control, but there is a part that we believe is within our control, within the control of the producers themselves. They propose by their plans to eliminate the factor by which those purchasing our products are able to bid one. against the other, gradually beating the price down until finally the weakest man accepts the lowest price, which is then set as the market price for the entire product.
We speak of the law of supply and demand, and I will admit at once that inherently and inevitably the law of supply and demand must function. But does it function? I have come to this conclusion, as have those for whom I speak, that the law of supply and demand can function only as between parties of equal strength. It cannot function as between organized purchasers on the one hand and unorganized agriculture on the other, no
more than it can function as between organized employers in industry and unorganized labour; hence the rise and growing strength of trade unions. If the law of supply and demand is to function it is necessary that there be some parity of bargaining power between the two parties who are doing business together.
As I have stated, the purpose and objective of the plans of which I have spoken is to create this sales department. We go a little further in these plans than voluntary cooperation of industry itself has gone. On the one hand these producers and the producers' boards have the power of licensing the trades which are dealing in their products, and anyone who is familiar with the trade dealing with poultry and live stock is aware of this that attached to that trade and an incubus upon it is what is known as the bootlegging section, those unethical operators who evade all laws, federal and provincial, and who will act in any way which may suit their purposes which are to bring to themselves greater profit -operators who are the curse of the trade and of those dealing with the trade. Only through some power of licensing can we confine the handling of our products to those who are legitimately engaged in the business and carrying on the business in an ethical way for the advantage of producer and consumer. So licensing is necessary.
On the other end of the scale, we find that principle which is commonly referred to as that of compulsion. Compulsion, yes, in a degree; that is to say, the power of a substantial majority of any branch of the agricultural industry to lay down and to enforce the methods and regulations and practices under which their sales shall be made.
May I call this to your attention, Mr. Speaker-and it is something which is overlooked by many who are opposed to this legislation and to these plans: Compulsion is not brought into effect or exercised by governments or by government officials or by (he state or by anyone save the majority of those who are engaged in that same line of industry; and who else has a better right? It is the expansion into the field of farm marketing of the democratic principle which is accepted in almost every field of human endeavour, namely, the right of a majority to lay down the rules under which society shall be governed, and to force, if necessary, the minority to obey those rules. I will ask you, Mr. Speaker, what development could ever have taken place, what organizations could have been achieved under civilization- could even civilization itself been brought about-had not that rule been applied?
The Address-Mr. Speakman

Democracy does not mean the unrestricted right of the individual to do as he likes. Democracy, I say again, implies the right of a majority within a community in any country and in any industry to lay down the rules and regulations under which that industry shall function. And this compulsion, so called, can be exercised only in the interests of the producers themselves, of those engaged in that particular industry; because anything which will redound to the benefit of the great majority must inevitably redound to the benefit of all. All sell on equal terms, all sell in the same markets, all are affected by the same conditions, and all receive the same advantages. So much for that.
The next thing to which I should like to call your attention, sir, is a question which has been discussed very widely throughout this country, namely, the capacity of the producer to handle and administer his own business on so gigantic a scale. Those who are opposed to this plan-I do not mean politically opposed; I am speaking now of those who are economically opposed because their interests may be affected deleteriously, those who have been battening upon and profiting from the farming industry-these people question the administrative ability of the farmer himself to handle this business. They say in effect that all the experience, all the wisdom and knowledge of market conditions are to be found in the ranks of those who are at present carrying on that business; that is, in the ranks of those who are doing the packing and processing and dealing in these various products. They have intimated that during all these years they have been acting in the interests of the producer. They have been functioning as the producers' sales agents, and they say that the interests and advantage of the producer have been their chief motive. To that I simply answer that you can judge the efficiency of men only by the results which they have achieved, and if those at present engaged in this business have been acting to the best of their ability in the interests of the producer, then, when under their administration we see the conditions which have been brought about and which are familiar to everyone here, conditions which are depressing and ruining the agricultural industry, I can only say, Mr. Speaker, that the producers of Canada are not unduly impressed by their assumption of efficiency, and they feel that a few years more of that kind of efficiency will see the live stock and poultry producers put out of business. They are, therefore, prepared to take over that responsibility. They believe, and they have [Mr. Speakman.J
so stated, that the only men really familiar with the problem are those who live with it; that the only men genuinely interested in the solution of the problem are those whom it affects; that the only men who can really understand and put into effect beneficial policies are those in whose interests such policies shall be administered and those who have lived with and understood those problems and suffered from a lack of their solution. They are prepared, therefore, to put these remedial policies into effect.
May 1 say also that two of our cattle men came down to Ottawa, representing the live stock producers, in order to present their plans. They included the largest single producer in Alberta-and when I say in Alberta that means in Canada-a rancher who runs about 12,000 head of stock. At present he is the chairman of our board. With him was the manager of the largest and most successful cooperative in our province dealing in live stock products. Those men came into contact with some of the leading men in this city, men in the highest branches of the civil service, men in government and business circles, and everyone who met them formed the impression that they were men competent to administer any business with which they were familiar, men competent to deal with, to handle and to control their own affairs. Indeed it is not too much to say that any man who has carried on the live stock industry for thirty-five years without going absolutely bankrupt is a business man of very high efficiency indeed, and is quite competent to deal with any further problems in respect of his own industry. That, at least, is the opinion of the producers, themselves, both of live stock and poultry.
Naturally I have discussed with those boards what their policies and objectives should be. I find that, with unanimous voice, they fully realize the limitations placed upon them. They realize that the final effective factor in connection with prices received is the ability and willingness of the consumer to buy and consume their goods. Their objective is not to sell a part of their product at a high price and restrict consumption, but to sell all their products at a reasonable price. Their objective is not to enhance the price to the consumer, but to eliminate the chaos and the losses incident to the manner in which their business is now carried on; to eliminate many of the charges and so-called services; to eliminate or control many of the exorbitant profits, and to secure for the producer his rea-

The Address-Mr. Speakman
sonable and legitimate share of the consumers' dollar.
But may I suggest this to you, Mr. Speaker. Assuming that this plan did raise the prices of some commodities to the consumer, as perhaps it might; I do not know, but supposing it did; I am going to ask any man in this house who is familiar with labour conditions to say when labour in this country was in the best position. Was it during the time the farmers were receiving little or nothing for their products, or was it during those periods when the farmers were receiving fair prices and therefore were in a position to buy the products of their toil? 1 ask any labour man or any business man; I think anyone will say. if he is an honest man-and most of us are-that the country is always more prosperous, wages are always more satisfactory and work is always more plentiful when the farmer is receiving a fair remimeration. That is all they anticipate; that is their objective; that is all they are asking. That is the purpose of their organization.
I think there is no man in this country who is familiar with conditions, no business man, no producer of farm or other products, no citizen of Canada and above all no member of this parliament who would not welcome and support anything which, legitimately and properly put into effect, would improve the situation of the agriculturist. I think it is recognized as one of the outstanding facts of this time that any policy, sound in principle, properly administered, which would improve that position and raise that standard is one which should merit the support and cooperation of everyone. But I am going to ask this further question; if I repeat it, it is because of its importance. Who is the man best qualified to say what measures will bring about that situation? It is the producer himself, and under the terms of every plan suggested it is only if the majority of the producers have come to that opinion as their confirmed and settled belief that those plans will become operative. I would ask every man who is a good citizen-and that embraces every member here-to leave it to the producers, to give them every encouragement to cooperate and organize and to support them if those producers come to the confirmed opinion. I think that is not too much to ask.
Other questions, of course, arise in connection with the details of such plans, and care is being taken in that regard by those who have drawn up and presented them, since they all are producers. No one save a legitimate producer may have a place on the board; every member has had years of experience in the business. They know the intricacies of the 92582-7
trade, and plans are carefully drawn in detail to meet the minor difficulties which might arise. For example, in connection with poultry care has been taken that nothing shall interfere with the mutually beneficial trade carried on between the producer and the individual consumer, that sale of poultry, eggs and so forth which is made directly by the producer to the consumer. It is true that those carrying on such trade must secure a permit from the board, a permit which costs nothing and which, in the words of the plan, may not be unreasonably withheld. Anyone familiar with the business will recognize the necessity for that permit system, because without it, under the guise of selling directly to the consumer the bootlegging trade would find its source of supply. In connection with breeding, hatching, incubating and all that sort of thing, all the details are taken care of and the proper exemptions made. The purpose is not to interfere with that business; the purpose-and these plans specifically set out that purpose- is to deal with and control the product which comes on the commercial market, that and no more.
In connection with poultry, if these plans come into operation the poultry producers may reasonably anticipate real success, for the three prairie provinces provide the entire surplus in Canada for interprovincial and export trade so far as poultry and poultry products are concerned. Other provinces, large producers, consume more than they produce and must import, and the total surplus is found in those three provinces. That augurs well for success if these three provinces coordinate their efforts.
In connection with live stock the situation is somewhat more complex, but I am sure that if these plans fructuate and achieve success, even if it is only a modicum of the results which reasonably might be anticipated, you will find throughout Canada a gradual movement towards that organization until, for the first time, we will have a national policy in dealing with live stock, which this nation has lacked in the past and the want of which has been so deleterious to our national wellbeing.
Someone asked about wheat. I am not discussing wheat, which, with its enormous sales on the world market, stands in a different position to that of any other farm product. I am speaking of live stock, of poultry and of dairy products, the organization of which will follow the organization of the first two commodities if they succeed. I am speaking of those commodities in which, in each case, you will find from ninety-five per cent, to ninety-eight per cent of the entire product sold within Canada. I should like to ask

The Address-Mr. Speakman

this question:	Why should the Canadian
market be demoralized and brought to chaos; why should Canadian farmers be ruined in connection with ninety-five per cent of their market for the sake of the five per cent exported? Our producers will have to extend their export trade. They purpose, through their own organization and their own efforts, to put forth various improvements as to grading standards and quality, and as to assurance to the customer, which is lacking at present, that when he pays for a number one article he can be sure of receiving that article. No government law or regulation so far has been able to bring about that result.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I should like to appeal to this house and to the country to give sympathetic consideration to the efforts of those producers who, under the authority of law, now for the first time are striving to bring themselves out of their difficulties and place themselves upon an equality with other industries, and to make a real contribution to the welfare of Canada. I need not perhaps appeal to the producers to consult their own best interests, not to listen exclusively to those in the trade benefiting by the troubles, benefiting by the chaos, who are the instigators and promoters of every petition which so far I have read and which has been presented to the producers for their signatures against the plan. I suggest that they study the plan on its own merits, make up their own minds, and vote in their own interests.

speechtext:
The Address-Mr. Mitchell
gets into power by trading on the disabilities and weaknesses of the party in power. There is nothing new about that; we have seen it in countries quite close to us, and in other parts [DOT]of the British dominions. I have no qualms in saying that I have come definitely to the opinion, having taken some part in the movements of the working people of this dominion, that we do not care who does it so long as it is done. We must not miss the opportunity; if this is the psychological moment when the foundation stone-merely the foundation stone -of these reforms is to be laid, then we should avail ounselves of it. If the government of the day can be the instrument of policy for the launching of these reforms, God speed them! That is why the addresses of the Prime Minister created such a profound effect upon the Canadian people; not because his suggestions were new, or came through some divine vision, but because of their source and the time at which they were enunciated. The Prime Minister said very definitely-perhaps it is a bad habit for men in public life to say these things too definitely; we have seen that in the last couple of days- that the old order is gone never to return'; that the time for reform and government control and regulation has come. He said, I gave a promise in 1930 to end unemployment, and by that I stand." He will have to get a move on. Then to give effect to this program he enunciated the following policy:
Establishment throughout Canada of a uniform wage and a uniform maximum working week;
Abolition of child labour and sweatshop conditions;
Creation of a permanent system of sound and scientific unemployment insurance and abolition of the dole;
Present obsolete Old Age Pensions Act to be replaced by a new, scientific scheme of old age pensions;
Health, accident and sickness insurance to be developed;
Further taxation of non-producers who derive their incomes from securities, mortgages and other wages of money;
Protection against exploitation of producers by monopolistic purchasers and certain types of middlemen and' distributors who are "economic parasites";
For consultation with other groups and the establishment of a national economic council.
What has been the reaction to the speeches of the Prime Minister? Some people say that the promises and the projected policy of the leader of the government stand in the same relationship to his political program as those of 1930. Some say that the policies enunciated smack of fascism, some say they are bolshevism, and one of the ministers of one

of our provincial governments said they are pure Marxism. I have had some experience among radical thinkers in this country and in the old land and can count on my fingers the number of men who have been able to wade through the three volumes of Marx. Frankly I believe that these last observations were merely a smoke screen to frustrate the possibility of forward movement by this House of Commons. I speak now of all the political parties; because the government has enunciated its policy, the leader of the opposition has agreed with him in connection with these suggested measures, and I am doing the same thing, so it seems we are almost in line for a national government. I am not making that as a suggestion, but merely as an observation. There is not a great deal to fight about, on the principles at least.
The other day I was reading the autobiography of Philip Snowden. I do not often quote from books in the House of Commons, but after the nasty names that have been given to the Prime Minister, it might be just as well to read this. This happened before Philip fell from grace; I am speaking of the time when he fell from grace from the viewpoint of many of the active Labour lights in the old country. This was before he went to the great beyond in the House of Lords; it was when he was a real radical in Great Britain, and it just shows how hard the way of the reformer is. I quote:
The views on the budget-
This is speaking of the historic budget of Lloyd George of some years ago when some of the reforms we have in mind to-day were introduced in the British House of Commons.
The views on the budget expressed in the lobby after Mr. Lloyd George sat down were very diverse. The Labour party welcomed the budget as the first real effort the government had made to grapple with the problem of wealth and poverty. Many Liberal members did not conceal their dismay at the prospect opened up by Mr. Lloyd George's first essay in finance.
That reads pretty true in connection with some of my friends on the other side-I am not speaking of members of the house-if the newspapers are to be believed.
One Liberal member, who considered the budget from the point of view of how it was going to touch his pocket, declared grimly: "He will never introduce another budget! His reputation is gone."
No budget in prewar days ever exposed so many vulnerable points of attack. It was bound to excite the bitter opposition of a large number of vested interests. The opposition of the income taxpayers would be incurred by the proposed increase in the tax.

The Address-Mr. Mitchell
The liquor interests would fight the increase in the licence duties to the utmost of their powers. One brewer asserted that these increased licences would mean ruin to half the brewers of the country!
They are still doing pretty well over there.
The city was up in arms against the increases in the stamp duties, and, of course, the landed interests were infuriated by the proposed land taxes. Next morning the press took a party view of the budget. It was denounced in the Tory newspapers without reserve under such headings as "the Red Flag Budget."
That sounds familiar.
The Liberal newspapers in their commendation of the budget varied according to the degree of their radicalism. One thing everybody agreed upon, that the budget was so controversial that it was doubtful if it would be carried without modifications.
We might almost imagine this written in the month of January in the year of Our Lord 1935.

speechtext:
That was in 1911.
The Labour party gave a warm welcome to the budget, and their general support to it was assured. We regarded it as chiefly noteworthy because it was largely based on the idea that socially created wealth must contribute more generously to national purposes.
I have always maintained that men are the instruments of policies and not policies the instruments of men. Frankly, I believe Lloyd George will go down in the history of the British commonwealth as one of its greatest statesmen in the last fifty years. He practically redistributed the wealth of Great Britain through the instrumentality of the social insurances without any of the consequences that to-day are visible in many of the countries of Europe. What I like about him is that he did things; he moved. I know one classic example of a prime minister of Great Britain who, in my judgment, attained that office on the basis of his good looks and poetry. When he got the instrument of policy in his hands he did not know what to do with it and he had to go over to the Tories to help him out. One does not need any imagination to know who that was. I have always maintained that you cannot justify inefficiency or lack of action on the basis of good intentions.
I want to say this also very frankly to the government, that if for some reason this might be merely the instrument of getting into power again, they are tampering with the very democratic institutions of this country. The working people and farmers of the dominion have been very patient under the adverse circumstances through which they
have passed, because after all is said and done they were not responsible for the depression; they were not consulted about it. Those who thought the stacks of paper they had in 1928 represented real wealth were, of course, badly disappointed. As I have said before, the inevitable windstorm came along and blew it out on to the street. That was inevitable, because unless the operatives in our industrial and agricultural life can buy back the products of their labour, I do not care what policy any government initiates, we are bound to pass through periods of very severe depressions such as we are passing through at the moment. After all, the real wealth of this and every other country can be expressed only in the ability of its people to engage in productive labour to such an extent and of such a character as to permit them to buy back the products of their labour.
I cannot at this time pursue a discussion of the various proposed measures except to say that while at the moment I am agreeing with them in principle, of course I reserve the right to criticize the details. I am not unmindful of the tribulations that surrounded the development of unemployment insurance in Great Britain and, for that matter, in every other country in which it has been established. Those who in their unguarded moments think unemployment insurance is a solution of the unemployment problem are just kidding themselves, and we might as welt be frank about the matter. But I believe it is a constructive policy to meet the problem; of unemployment, to meet the very difficult situation in which the municipalities find themselves at the moment, the end of which has not of course yet been reached. Whatever system exists, some insurance against the ravages of unemployment is necessary, because change in its very essence under any system of government creates an unemployment problem. Last year when I was in Great Britain they celebrated the twenty-first anniversary of the doctrine of social insurance by a dinner given to Mr. Lloyd George at which were represented the leaders of all political thought in Great Britain. It is necessary sometimes to say these things in view of the enthusiasm that has been developed in connection with certain forms of legislation, and I might point out that the British act has since its first passage undergone twenty-eight major operations. They have been moving in the direction of trial and error in their own way to make the legislation more nearly fit the needs of that country. I say this because I believe we must not get ourselves

The Address-Mr. Mitchell
into the mental condition that because we are setting in motion these policies, the very grave question of unemployment may be shelved and dismissed from the minds of the members of this house and other governmental institutions in this country. Some means must be found whereby we can tie up production to consumption; some means must be found whereby we can put a suit on a man's back and permit him to work and earn the necessary money to pay for it without its being an act of charity.
Comment has been made to the effect that the British North America Act stands in the way of many of these suggested policies. If such action is necessary I believe it is the duty of this government to seek the cooperation of the provincial governments. I hold the view that it is the patriotic duty-and I do not often use that word-of all governments in Canada to lend their aid towards bringing the British North America Act to the point where it may meet the requirements of the present century. I have no criticism to make of the framers of the act. They acted in the light of conditions existing at that time and possessing only that limited vision possible to mortal humans. They could not have contemplated the tremendous developments that have taken place in transportation, communication, industrialization and agriculture. To those who stand in the way of any movement towards amendment of the act I should like to say that after all is said and done it was passed for the benefit of the Canadian people; it was passed to meet their everyday needs and to make possible the legislative functions of government. With the changes in the functions of governments it is inevitable that there must be changes in our constitution. Among people from one end of Canada to the other the opinion is crystallized to the point where they believe one of the greatest requirements is the amending of the act.
I believe it was the leader of the opposition who raised the discussion concerning the Senate. I am making reference to all these points because I believe one would do better to put his finger on the spot where the sand may be put into the machinery. The right lion, gentleman has said that we have a Tory Senate. If I gather anything from the temper of the Canadian people, and if it is the policy of the Senate to put sand into the machinery, then we will have to reform the Senate. The time has long since passed when the Senate should be used as unemployment insurance for many of those in political life. I am of the opinion that anybody charged with preparing legislation should be responsible to our people. This has been a question of wide

discussion for many years; if I remember correctly both political parties have discussed it sympathetically. I am not making these observations in a spirit of criticism of members of the Senate, because I believe if they stand in the way of reform there will be plenty of time to do that.
I see that the time allotted to me has almost expired. In conclusion I should like to make one or two	observations.	It	hastaken me twenty-five years to learn some things; that is one of the tragedies of life. It takes us a long time to learn anything, and then we pass out	of	the picture and	our
children have to learn all over again.

a book. I remember a very good Liberal once saying to me, " Humphrey, never write a book." I do not think I ever will. I am not unmindful of	the part played	in	thehistory of this dominion by legislative bodies, nor do I forget the real progress which has been made since I came to this country about a generation ago.	I	want to say	to	the
labour men and farmers of Canada that there is no substitution for organization among those engaged in their occupation. To the working people I say there is no substitution for a free trade union. Lawyers and doctors learned that many years ago. If the Canadian people think that by giving three cheers at a political meeting their problems may be ended, they are only fooling themselves. It is essential that people vitally interested in the passing of certain legislation should have some form of organization capable of speaking for them, one which can take care of the changes found necessary to protect their interests. No matter how good the intentions of the government may be, it is quite necessary that through organizations interested parties attend to their own well being and destiny. We have seen that on many occasions. I believe the leader of the opposition referred to the vocational education bill; if some organization had been interested in carrying out the policies laid down in that legislation, something might have been done, and that applies to all legislation.
I should like to state that I will support the proposed reforms so long as they are in conformity with the opinions I have long held. And may I add that I would be most unfair if I failed to congratulate the government upon at least attempting to lay the foundation stone of reforms which have been successfully carried out in other sections of the British commonwealth

Mr. Speaker, while agreeing entirely and unreservedly with the suggestion to shorten the debate, made by the leader of the opposition, may I be pardoned if for a few moments I take the time of the house? Once more the views I wish to express are not those of any party or group in the chamber, but they are held by a number of people, difficult to count and living in all parts of the country, who consider me as their representative.
I do not purpose entering into a consideration of the various subjects contained in the speech from the throne. When they appear before us in the form of bills I shall register my votes and perhaps express my opinions in connection with them. The idea of speaking to-night has been suggested to me not so much through arguments urged in this debate as by the impression created on my mind by the two remarkable addresses of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) respectively. That impression I propose to state frankly to them and to their friends; not that any feeling I may have is of any importance, but because I sincerely believe that my reaction is that of a large number of people throughout the country, whether they belong to one party or the other, or to no party at all.
I have listened to the whole speech of the leader of the opposition, and to part of that of the Prime Minister, and I propose to read carefully to-morrow the rest of it. As to my friend the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group I unfortunately did not have the pleasure of hearing him, but I shall read his speech also. Only, a little while after he had taken his seat, a friend of mine, not belonging to his group, told me: "Woods-worth has spoken and has been very reasonable," which did not surprise me. Seeing that the leader of the government is rapidly preparing for the evolution of the Tory party towards socialism and that the leader of the Liberal party is inviting the leader of the Tory party to join his ranks in order to enhance Tory socialism, I suppose my friend to my left (Mr. Woodsworth) is preparing to lead the remaining Conservative forces of Canada; all of which shows that political principles and programs are very changeable things indeed. But let us leave that for the time being.
May I say, first, that I am a sincere and personal friend of both leaders? I have known both for many years. I really believe that I know them more intimately perhaps than many of their followers. For them both I have an equal sympathy and admiration. I have known the leaders of parliament and of government in this country for forty
years. As a boy I assisted in the galleries of the old parliament to the last encounter between Sir John A. Macdonald and the then new leader of the Liberal party, Mr. Laurier. In the years following, as a member of the house, I have been a witness to the debates led by Laurier on the one side and Tupper on the other, and then Borden and the able men accompanying him. After having left parliament I still followed the course of men and things pretty closely. Now I say with all sincerity that, although Macdonald and Laurier may stand high above the other statesmen we have had in this confederation since its inception, we have not possessed two abler men, two men more sincere in their respective ideas and policies, or tiwo men more capable of giving service to tiheir country, than the Prime Minister and the leader of the apposition. I believe equally in tiheir sincerity; but I must tell botlh of them and their followers quite frankly that the number of people who are ceasing to believe in the sincerity of their leaders and of public men generally is fast increasing. If the debates that are going to take place in this house, as a preface to the debates that will take place before the nation in the next few months, are to be carried on in the same manner, with the same bitterness, with the same attacks and counter-attacks between the leaders and followers of both parties, the respect of the nation for its leaders and the belief of all sincere Liberals, Conservatives and independents in the sincerity of party leaders will fast diminish.
I have not heard by radio the five speeches which the Prime Minister delivered preceding the session. I never listen to the radio; I have none. But I have read those speeches most carefully. I have annotated them for my own use and benefit; and I am free to admit now what I will repeat elsewhere, if necessary, that they contain much that is good, many suggestions which I hope will be adopted by parliament, whatever party is in power, and carried out for the benefit of the people of Canada.
It has been suggested that the Prime Minister is not sincere and that this is only preelectoral talk. I hold no brief for the Prime Minister. I am glad for five minutes that he is not here. I am not a follower of his. I have fought, his policies in the past; but when I hear his sincerity being challenged I feel bound to protest. Not only do I believe, but I know that he is sincere. He may have been mistaken in having waited so long to suggest these reforms. Some of them stand in dire contrast to the policies of his party and his

The Address-Mr. Bourassa
own policies in the past; but I know that these thoughts have been in his mind for months and for years; and when it is suggested all over the country that the Prime Minister is a selfish financier, associated with St. James street, and that this is only a smoke screen to prevent other parties from bringing in true social reforms, I know it is untrue. I know that the pontiffs in the financial circles of Montreal and elsewhere dread the effective power of R. B. Bennett, if I may be pardoned for naming him, more than that of any other man.
But that being said, I am bound to say that, after reading his speeches, I deeply deplored the observations made by the Prime Minister against the leader of the opposition. He has spoiled his own argumentation. He has diminished himself and his policy; and moreover he has been unfair to an opponent who is equally worthy of respect with himself. The leader of the opposition I have known for a longer time than the Prime Minister. With some of his policies, I have both agreed and disagreed. As to his sincerity in the views which he held long before he was a member of the house, when he was the youngest official in the service of this country, I know how sincerely bent he was in bringing about reforms in the social and economic structure of this country. Much laughter has been raised in this house because the leader of the opposition said: " Nineteen years ago I wrote a book." I suppose the joke will go on. No wonder. If a Conservative had said the same thing-

speechtext: It takes a real man to write a good book.

speechtext:
Pardon me if I give it in my own way-my Liberal friends would have exploded with laughter, just as the Tories did when the leader of the opposition said that. Will that little and cheap joke take 'with the people of Canada? Maybe. We are the worthy representatives of a young and childish nation that makes much noise over very little thinking. It is but too unfortunate that we have so few men in the service of the nation who have had the intelligence and the energy, the knowledge and the proper study to write books from which, from whatever source they come, we coidd derive some useful information. There are names standing in the annals of all nations, of people who never did anything but write books, and some of them only one book; yet from that one book flowed rivers of thought which inspired men of action. Great matters of policy, national or international, social or economic, are attributed by the casual reader of history to this politician cr that, to this business man or that great captain

of industry; but the original thought creating those reforms will be found, by those at least who know how to read, in some one book or perhaps in some speech.
Not only that; not only has the leader of the opposition done service to the country by writing that book. By his acts, first, as a humble servant of the crown, then, later on, as a member of his party and as leader of the government, he has done many things in conformity with his principles. The Conservative party would lose nothing of the credit due them on account of the mental energy, the true and proven patriotism of their leader and, I say without hesitation, his disinterestedness-and I insist on the word because of the prejudices that have been broadcast from Cape Breton to British Columbia against what is perhaps the most admirable quality of that man-by admitting that the leader of the Liberal party is also a good Canadian who has done service to his country.
That is what I have had in my heart, because I love both of them; but I have had another thought in mind also. The more I travel and come in contact with people of all races and creeds in this country, the more I am convinced that what I am now going to say, as next to the dean of this house, is a bit of useful and friendly advice to all hon. members. We are on the eve of a general election. Within a few months this country will be flooded with oratory, over the radio, with articles in newspapers and speeches of various kinds on all the platforms of this country. It will be called "appealing to the reason of the people," but hon. gentlemen must admit that the average politician-and I have committed this sin long enough myself to confess it- does not appeal to reason. He usually appeals to sentiment and interest, and unfortunately these two chords are much more responsive than reason, conscience or intelligence, even in the triumph of democracy which is very often the triumph of stupid mobocracy. Well, what I have to say to my Liberal friends is that they have the chance of their lives to do their country a service which perhaps their party has not been able to do before. You know you are going to win this election.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

speechtext:
Of course; it would be
ridiculous not to admit it. You know you are going to sweep the country. As a personal friend of the leader of the opposition I said to him at the end of last session; "My dear friend, I am praying to God that you do not come back with too big a majority!"

The Address-Mr. Bourassa
Therefore what reason could you have, from even the smallest, narrowest or basest point of view, to carry on a campaign of slander, of bitter attacks against Bennett, Cahan, or this one or that one? I would go further, or perhaps lower down: what interest would you have in carrying the election in the same way that your opponents carried the election five years ago? The main reason which will bring about the defeat of the Conservative party will not be the policy of the government. On the whole I think their policy has been fairly good. I will go further:	because of the
mental power, the energy, the persistency and, I repeat, the personal disinterestedness of the Prime Minister, the policy has been better than it would have been if the government had been led by an ordinary man; and it has not been as bad as it could have been, having regard to the past record and principles of the Tory party. So I repeat the question; why will they be snowed under this summer? It will not be because of their policy. It will be because there are thousands and hundreds of thousands of people in this country who will not listen to argument or Reason; they will simply say; "We trusted the Tories in 1930. They deceived us. We do not trust them any more." That will determine the votes of thousands of men and women all over the country. Not only will the Liberals who voted for the Tory candidates five years ago return to the fold; many Conservatives will do the same thing in connection with this government that many Liberals did in connection with the Liberal government in 1930.
I am sorry for that, in a sense. I hope I will have nothing to do with the election, that I will be altogether out of the scrap. My sincere wish for the welfare of the country would be that one party or the other, it does not matter to me which, should be returned with a very small majority and that a sufficient number of members should be returned in this corner to hold the balance. I do not say they should blackmail the government. There ought to be enough intelligent men among them to realize that a blackmailing minority may gain something immediately, in one way or another, but that it soon loses the confidence of the people. If they also consider the possibility of one or two of their leaders becoming associated with the reigning party, either by going into the cabinet or becoming members of the Senate, as happened to two or three of the past leaders of the Progressive party, they will soon realize why, having come to this parliament some 69 in
number in 1921, they dwindled down to the number returned at the last election.
As an old man, an old Canadian and, may I say, as a Christian, my appeal to all my colleagues is this: Let us resolve now to carry on this campaign, first in this house and later throughout the country, in a broad spirit of citizenship and Christianity. It can be done. You should do it in your own interests. You need not sacrifice the basic principle in your policies, if such thing exists; you need not sacrifice any article of your program, or to use the American slang expression, any plank in your platform. You could suggest your arguments to the people and endeavour to prove that your policy is better than the other, without saying that the other party have never done anything good, without saying that your opponents are not sincere, without saying, as the Tories did in 1930, that the Liberals had done nothing for the people during ten years and that the Conservatives alone could save the country. They ought to have known then, as I said last year in this very chamber, that no party, no man, either yesterday or ten years ago, or to-morrow, or five or ten years hence, could or can save the country through the efforts and cooperation alone of men belonging to one party, if they antagonize the rest of the country or create such a feeling of bitterness in their opponents that in their turn those opponents will profit by any accident of political fortune, or by any crisis, economic, social or international, to turn the game against them.
That brings me back to my starting point, which will be my conclusion. My Liberal friends will win. But I say to them, make no mistake. The votes that will be added to your actual majorities, the votes that will give you back the constituencies which you have lost, and many others, will not be given to you because the confidence of the country in the Liberal party has been restored. It will be one of the last tests, perhaps the last test which a rapidly increasing number of Canadians will make of the party system. If you win this election by outdoing your opponents, by promising to undo all that they have done and to replace it by perfection ; if you win the election by promising more butter than bread, when the people come to realize, two or three years from now, that it is the same old story, then you, Liberals, as the Tories four years ago, will have done more not to advance the interests of this group, the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, but to further social unrest and future revolutions and true bolshevism, which lies not at the door of my friend from Win-

The Address-Mr. Bourassa
mpeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) but at the door of the true communists who have been continually attacking that hon. gentlemen, whom they rightly regard as the most effective obstacle to social revolution. That advice which I have already given I offer especially to my good friends from the province of Quebec or, broadly speaking, to my French and Catholic fellow members. To them I say: In the principles of your faith, in the traditions of your race, to which so many of tlhe leaders of this country, of Protestant faith and of British origin, have rendered testimony, in these two great moral forces there lies your greatest strength to save the country. And it is acknowledged now. I was reading only to-day an admirable pamphlet issued by a social committee of the United Church in Toronto, a pamphlet which I commend to the reading of every member of this house. It is published under the signature of Sir Robert Falconer and of the secretary, whose name I forget. I shall write to them as a Canadian and as a Christian, thanking them for that admirable program of social reform. What pleased me profoundly was to find therein a paragraph endorsing the opinions expressed by Pope Pius XI in his great encyclical. Do you not see that tremendous spiritual force, which has been dormant in Canada for so many years, now rising? Could the old men in this house imagine that a time would come when a gathering of Methodist or Presbyterian ministers would render testimony to the teachings of the Pope in Rome? I am afraid that some of my dear old friends of the house in the past must have trembled in their tombs, some of those stout leaders of the Orange order, if they have read an expression of opinion, in the name of the whole United Church, endorsing the views held by the Anglican bishops in Lambeth Palace last year and the views expressed by the Pope.
Now are we, responsible in some sense to the people of Canada for their spiritual and moral welfare as well as for their material good, going to neglect that tremendous spiritual upheaval? Nothing is further from my thought than to suggest that any party should exploit the opinions either of the Pope or of the United Church or of any other church for party ends. I have always deprecated the introduction of religion into politics 

which unfortunately has been done for so many years in this country by all parties- by making use of clerics or of clerical opinions as a means of bringing votes to one party or another. It is a thing to be despised and condemned. But surely the spiritual forces which might be used to bring the people of 
Canada to think of these matters, social and economic, from the highest point of view, a point of view higher than the mere material interest of the labourer, the working man, the merchant or the land owner, should be considered rather than neglected by all men responsible for the laws and the government of this country.
Would it not be possible for the Conservatives to expound their program and for the Liberals to expound theirs without bitterly attacking one another? It is perfectly fair for the Liberals to say, as my friend from East Hamilton (Mr. Mitchell) said to-night, that a good deal of the reforms proposed by the government can be laid at the door of their own party and that therefore they should be given credit for them. That is quite legitimate. It is quite legitimate for the Liberals to point out to the electors that promises made in 1930 have not been fulfilled. It is quite legitimate for the Conservatives to reply that their task has been rendered much more difficult because of the lack of vision of the Liberal government prior to 1930-and it would be quite true. I well remember that during the session of 1930, I, as a humble independent member, warned some of the Liberal ministers against the dangers that were coming-the depression, unemployment and the crisis. I told them that they ought to take means right then to meet that situation. But no; it was a small passing matter; Dunning would settle that in his little budget. Well, that delusion was as great as the delusion of the Conservatives at the present time, that the sole pronouncement made by the Prime Minister is going to save them from the consequences of their language in 1930. Chickens come home to roost every time; sometimes it takes four years and sometimes ten years, but they always come back.

If my friend knew
something more about the political history of the country he would know that I fought Laurier when he was at the height of his popularity. When the Tory party was denouncing him from the Atlantic to the Pacific as the instrument of Catholicism and French domination, I stood by him. When he was the idol of Quebec, I stood almost alone against him in defence of the principles for which I have fought all my life. But when

The Address-Mr. Thompson (Lanark)
he was betrayed by his Liberal friends, when he was downtrodden during the war, I came to him and1 freely tendered him a helping hand, not to carry but to go through the elections of 1917. But since I have been provoked by a gentleman who may or may not be in his senses I will add this. The last letter which Laurier wrote in his own hand, he wrote to me, to express his sympathy for the most cruel bereavement I have had during my life; and the answyer I wrote came to him the day after his attack and two days before his death. But he knows now that although I fought him because of differences in principle, I loved him all my life; and he knew it then. The day I passed in his house in 1917, when he wras betrayed by men whom he had covered with honours and favours-I never received anything from him and never asked-that day he pressed me on his bosom and said to me: " Bourassa, what has happened to me to-day you predicted eleven years ago. I know now where my true friends are to be found." May I be pardoned for having disclosed that feeling of intimacy? Perhaps much may be pardoned to an old man in his closing days; but this is as sincere as the sentiments I have expressed with regard to the present Prime Minister and the present leader of the opposition. If I go out of public life with one feeling, with one conviction, it is this: a deep regret for many bitter words that I have used in my life, deep and sincere repentance for all my violences of language; but I hope they will be forgiven me by God and man because not once in my life have I attacked anybody unjustly, from my point of view at least, and without believing it was my duty to do so.	.
